Pekahiah
pek-uh-HYE-uh
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Peqachyah (H6494) — "Yahweh has opened (the eyes)" or "Yahweh-opened." From paqach ("to open the eyes") + Yah. The name's positive theological content sits ironically on a king whose eyes were closed to the very Yahweh his name confessed.

📖 Biblical Definition

Pekahiah (c. 742 — 740 BC) was the seventeenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 15:22-26), son of Menahem and only known successor to him. His two-year reign was the briefest possible stability in the chaotic post-Jehu period: he continued his father's golden-calf apostasy, continued his father's Assyrian-tribute policy, and was assassinated in the palace at Samaria by his own military commander Pekah son of Remaliah along with fifty Gileadite soldiers from his own bodyguard. The Chronicler's framing emphasizes the inside-job nature of the coup: 'Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites: and he killed him, and reigned in his room' (2 Kings 15:25). Pekahiah's two-year reign and palace-coup death continued the pattern of usurpation-without-mandate that defined the northern kingdom's last thirty years. Six kings in thirty years (Zachariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, Hoshea); four of them assassinated.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Seventeenth king of Israel (c. 742-740 BC); son of Menahem; reigned 2 years; assassinated in the palace at Samaria by his own military commander Pekah son of Remaliah with 50 Gileadite soldiers.

PEKAHIAH, proper noun. Hebrew Peqachyah (H6494) — "Yahweh has opened (the eyes)," from paqach + Yah.

Seventeenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 742-740 BC); son of Menahem.

Two-year reign; continued his father's apostasy and Assyrian-tribute policy.

Assassinated in the palace at Samaria by Pekah son of Remaliah with 50 Gileadite soldiers (2 Kings 15:25).

Distinct from Pekah his assassin (similar-sounding but distinct Hebrew name).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Kings 15:23-24 — "In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah Pekahiah the son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned two years. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD: he departed not from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin."

2 Kings 15:25 — "But Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites: and he killed him, and reigned in his room."

Hosea 7:7 — "They are all hot as an oven, and have devoured their judges; all their kings are fallen: there is none among them that calleth unto me."

Proverbs 28:2 — "For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Pekahiah is corrupted when his two-year reign is treated as a forgettable interlude rather than as one more link in the divided-monarchy collapse chain, when his name's irony is overlooked, or when the Gileadite-conspiracy detail in the assassination is missed as evidence of the depth of palace disloyalty.

expand to see more

Forgettable-interlude misreading. Pekahiah's two-year reign sits between his more prominent father Menahem and his more prominent assassin Pekah. Many Bible surveys skip him entirely. The narrator's careful inclusion preserves the canonical evidence of the systematic collapse: six kings in thirty years was not random instability but the working-out of long-pronounced prophetic judgment (Hos 7:7; 8:4). Each individual reign matters because each link in the chain shows the same pattern.

Gileadite-conspiracy detail. 2 Kings 15:25 includes the specific detail that Pekah's conspiracy was carried out 'with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites.' Argob and Arieh are otherwise unknown; the fifty Gileadites are revealing. Gilead was the trans-Jordanian region of Israel that had been the home territory of Jephthah and of the Tishbite Elijah; under the divided monarchy it had remained Israelite. The Gileadite participation in the palace coup against Pekahiah signals that even the most distant Israelite tribes had abandoned dynastic loyalty by this point. The kingdom's internal cohesion was gone.
